steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on automatically generating question-answer datasets for long-tail knowledge, where tail entities are defined using Wikidata. Motivate why LLMs struggle with tail entities, explain our approach and the challenges of automatic generation, mention the GPT3 evaluation, and end with a contributions list.

- Long-tail problem

- Wikidata-based definition
  - main external resources: Wikipedia documents (cite), Wikidata knowledge graphs (cite)
  - tail-entity distribution determined by knowledge distributions in Wikipedia and Wikidata
  - our proposal: tail entities by degree information in Wikidata, not Wikipedia as in prior study (cite)
  - datasets with distributions different from previous works (cite) -> diversity in tail-knowledge QA
  - entity degree in Wikidata reflects engagement with general knowledge
- Automatic generation
  - building QA datasets needs a lot of human resources; blocks diverse datasets from various domains needed to test robustness
  - main emphasis: automatic generation of long-tail QA datasets
  - challenges: filtering noisy questions, question granularity, difficulty control, prompt engineering
  - need further research; presented through case studies to stimulate research

  - improving pretrained LLMs with external resources (external documents, knowledge graphs) at inference

  - code publicly available

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Open-domain Question Answering (QA) means answering questions about common knowledge, and it has been a challenging task for a long time in natural language understanding, information retrieval, and related fields. Large language models (LLMs) that are trained on internet text capture a wide range of world knowledge, both widely known facts and domain-specific information. These models have been very successful in QA tasks, and they do not need external documents during inference because they store the knowledge implicitly in their parameters.

But the impressive results of LLMs in QA tasks are mostly seen for common concepts that appear often on the internet (called "head entities"), which LLMs are more likely to learn well during pre-training. On the other hand, for long-tail knowledge, which includes entities that rarely occur (called "tail entities"), LLMs have trouble giving accurate answers and they often hallucinate. Since most QA datasets mainly focus on head entities, there has been limited research on how LLMs perform on long-tail knowledge. Recently, a study tried to bridge this gap by building dedicated QA datasets for tail entities. They used entity frequency in Wikipedia to define tail entities and showed quantitatively that LLMs are limited in handling such entities.

The main external resources that QA models get knowledge from are Wikipedia documents and Wikidata knowledge graphs. So the distribution of tail entities is mostly determined by how knowledge is distributed in Wikipedia and Wikidata. In this study we propose a new way to define tail entities, based on their degree information in Wikidata, unlike the earlier study which relies on Wikipedia. This way we generate QA datasets that have different distributions from previous works, which brings more diversity to tail-knowledge QA datasets. In Wikidata, the degree of an entity reflects how much it is engaged with general knowledge. That is why we use this degree information to define tail entities.

- Automatic generation
  - building QA datasets needs a lot of human resources; blocks diverse datasets from various domains needed to test robustness
  - main emphasis: automatic generation of long-tail QA datasets
  - challenges: filtering noisy questions, question granularity, difficulty control, prompt engineering
  - need further research; presented through case studies to stimulate research
- Evaluation and contributions
  - pretrained LLMs, specifically GPT3, on our tail entity datasets
  - patterns differ from prior work (cite) using Wikipedia -> importance of diverse QA sets
  - improving pretrained LLMs with external resources (external documents, knowledge graphs) at inference
  - link results to challenges in automatic generation
  - contributions: new tail-knowledge QA datasets from Wikidata; automatic construction + open challenges; GPT3 with/without external resources
  - code publicly available

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Open-domain Question Answering (QA) means answering questions about common knowledge, and it has been a challenging task for a long time in natural language understanding, information retrieval, and related fields. Large language models (LLMs) that are trained on internet text capture a wide range of world knowledge, both widely known facts and domain-specific information. These models have been very successful in QA tasks, and they do not need external documents during inference because they store the knowledge implicitly in their parameters.

But the impressive results of LLMs in QA tasks are mostly seen for common concepts that appear often on the internet (called "head entities"), which LLMs are more likely to learn well during pre-training. On the other hand, for long-tail knowledge, which includes entities that rarely occur (called "tail entities"), LLMs have trouble giving accurate answers and they often hallucinate. Since most QA datasets mainly focus on head entities, there has been limited research on how LLMs perform on long-tail knowledge. Recently, a study tried to bridge this gap by building dedicated QA datasets for tail entities. They used entity frequency in Wikipedia to define tail entities and showed quantitatively that LLMs are limited in handling such entities.

The main external resources that QA models get knowledge from are Wikipedia documents and Wikidata knowledge graphs. So the distribution of tail entities is mostly determined by how knowledge is distributed in Wikipedia and Wikidata. In this study we propose a new way to define tail entities, based on their degree information in Wikidata, unlike the earlier study which relies on Wikipedia. This way we generate QA datasets that have different distributions from previous works, which brings more diversity to tail-knowledge QA datasets. In Wikidata, the degree of an entity reflects how much it is engaged with general knowledge. That is why we use this degree information to define tail entities.

Building QA datasets usually needs a lot of human resources, and this makes it hard to create diverse datasets from various domains, which are essential to test how robust current QA models are. In this study our main focus is on generating long-tail QA datasets automatically. But we run into several challenges in this process, like filtering noisy questions, question granularity, difficulty control, and prompt engineering. These challenges need more research to find fundamental solutions. We present them through case studies, hoping to stimulate more research in this area and help the development of QA models.

Finally, we evaluate how pretrained LLMs, specifically GPT3, perform on our tail entity datasets. We find patterns that are different from prior work, which defines tail entities based on Wikipedia and not Wikidata. This shows that it is important to use diverse QA sets to measure the robustness of QA models accurately. We also look into strategies to improve the performance of pretrained LLMs by adding external resources, like external documents or knowledge graphs, at inference time on our automatically-generated long-tail QA datasets. We connect these experimental results with the challenges we ran into while generating the QA datasets automatically. To summarize, our contributions are:

- • New tail knowledge QA datasets that are derived from the Wikidata knowledge graph.

- • A description of how to construct QA datasets automatically and the open research challenges that come with it.

- • An evaluation of how GPT3 performs with and without external resources on our new datasets.

Our code is publicly available.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Open-domain Question Answering (QA) [1,2], which involves answering questions regarding common knowledge, has long been a challenging task in the fields of natural language understanding, information retrieval, and related domains [3,4]. Large language models (LLMs) trained on internet text capture a wide range of world knowledge, encompassing both widely known facts and domain-specific information. These models have achieved remarkable success in QA tasks, eliminating the need for external documents during inference by implicitly storing knowledge in their parameters [5,6,7].

However, the impressive achievements of LLMs in QA tasks are primarily observed with regard to common concepts that frequently appear on the internet (referred to as "head entities"), which are thus more likely to be learned well by LLMs during pre-training. Conversely, when it comes to dealing with long-tail knowledge, which encompasses rarely occurring entities (referred to as "tail entities"), LLMs struggle to give accurate answers and often hallucinate [8]. Due to the predominant focus of most QA datasets on head entities [2,1,9], research investigating the performance of LLMs on long-tail knowledge has been limited. Recently, [7] conducted a study to bridge this gap by constructing dedicated QA datasets for tail entities. Their approach used the entity frequency in Wikipedia to define tail entities and quantitatively demonstrating the limitations of LLMs in handling such entities.

Wikipedia documents [10] and Wikidata knowledge graphs [11] are the primary external resources from which QA models acquire knowledge. So the distribution of tail entities is largely determined by the knowledge distributions within Wikipedia and Wikidata. In this study, we propose a novel approach to defining tail entities based on their degree information in Wikidata, as opposed to [7] relying on Wikipedia. By doing so, we generate QA datasets with distinct distributions from previous works [7], thus fostering diversity within tail-knowledge QA datasets. In Wikidata, the degrees of entities reflect their level of engagement with general knowledge. Hence, we leverage this degree information to define tail entities.

The construction of QA datasets typically requires significant human resources, hindering the creation of diverse datasets from various domains that are essential for testing the robustness of current QA models. In this study, our main emphasis lies on the automatic generation of long-tail QA datasets. However, we run into several challenges in this process, such as filtering noisy questions, question granularity, difficulty control, and prompt engineering. These challenges necessitate further research to identify fundamental solutions. We present these challenges through case studies, aiming to stimulate additional research in this area and foster the development of QA models.

Lastly, we assess the performance of pretrained LLMs, specifically GPT3, on our tail entity datasets. Our findings show different patterns compared to prior work [7], which defines tail entities based on Wikipedia rather than Wikidata. This underscores the importance of utilizing diverse QA sets to accurately gauge the robustness of QA models. Moreover, we investigate strategies to enhance the performance of pretrained LLMs by incorporating external resources, such as external documents or knowledge graphs, during inference time on our automatically-generated long-tail QA datasets. We connect these experimental results with the challenges encountered during the automatic QA dataset generation process. In summary, our contributions encompass:

- • Introduction of novel tail knowledge QA datasets derived from the Wikidata knowledge graph.

- • Description of the automatic construction of QA datasets and the open research challenges that come with it.

- • Evaluation of GPT3’s performance with/without external resources on our new datasets.

Our code is publicly available 1.
